questions.statement: What is the purpose of this text?
questions.context: Text: 'This guide is for students starting their first year at university. It explains how to register, where to find the library and how to ask for help in English.'

options.text: To give practical instructions to new students
options.feedback: The text announces who it is for and lists the tasks it covers, which is the definition of a practical guide.

options.text: To persuade students to choose this university
options.feedback: Persuasion would require praise or a recommendation, and none appears.

options.text: To criticise the registration system
options.feedback: No complaint about the system is expressed anywhere in the text.

options.text: To compare two universities
options.feedback: Only one institution is mentioned, so no comparison is possible.

questions.explanation:
Purpose is usually stated in the first sentence of a short text and confirmed by the type of information it supplies. A list of tasks signals a guide, not an argument.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What tone does this text use?
questions.context: Text: 'A review in a weekly magazine describes the new restaurant as 'expensive, predictable and almost beside the point'.

options.text: Sarcastic and dismissive
options.feedback: Calling a restaurant 'predictable' and 'beside the point' while stating it is expensive conveys contempt in place of praise.

options.text: Enthusiastic and promotional
options.feedback: Promotion would use positive words, and every term here is negative.

options.text: Neutral and descriptive
options.feedback: A neutral description would not attach a dismissive phrase to the venue.

options.text: Indifferent and unemotional
options.feedback: The language is engaged and pointed, which is the opposite of indifference.

questions.explanation:
Tone is judged by word choice and by what a description implies. A review can be critical without being neutral, and here the vocabulary is chosen to dismiss.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the likely purpose of this text?
questions.context: Text: 'Our programme is the only one of its kind in the region. Enrolment is free. Spaces are limited.'

options.text: To persuade the reader to enrol before places run out
options.feedback: A claim of uniqueness, a removal of cost and a reminder of scarcity are the standard moves of a recruitment message.

options.text: To explain the academic content of the programme
options.feedback: No subject matter is described, so the text is not an academic description.

options.text: To warn readers against enrolling
options.feedback: Nothing discourages the reader; every stated fact encourages enrolment.

options.text: To report enrolment figures from last year
options.feedback: Figures from previous years are not given.

questions.explanation:
Purpose becomes clear from the combination of claims offered: a competitive advantage, the removal of an obstacle and the threat of scarcity together form an invitation to act.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the absence of independent testing suggest?
questions.context: Text: 'The manufacturer states that the product is safe. No independent test is mentioned anywhere in the report.'

options.text: The claim rests entirely on the manufacturer's own interest in reassuring buyers
options.feedback: With no external verification cited, the supporting evidence is the statement of the party that benefits from the claim.

options.text: The product has been tested by official laboratories
options.feedback: An independent test would have to be mentioned, and none is.

options.text: Independent testing was performed and found no problems
options.feedback: Nothing in the text indicates that testing occurred.

options.text: The report was written to criticise the manufacturer
options.feedback: The text reports a claim without attacking it, so it is not a critique.

questions.explanation:
Who supplies the evidence is part of evaluating a claim. A statement made by the party that benefits from it carries less weight until independent support appears.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What kind of writer is this?
questions.context: Text: 'A historian writes that the old customs house, now used as a museum, was for many years the busiest building in the town.'

options.text: A historian describing a building's past function
options.feedback: The reference to what happened for many years in the past describes a documented function.

options.text: A tourist brochure promoting a museum
options.feedback: A brochure would invite a visit and recommend the museum, and no invitation appears.

options.text: An architect describing a design
options.feedback: No architectural feature is described anywhere in the text.

options.text: A novelist inventing a scene
options.feedback: The sentence reports a fact about the past rather than narrating a fictional scene.

questions.explanation:
Purpose narrows when it is read together with the register and the kind of detail supplied. A past-tense factual description signals history, while an invitation signals promotion.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What tone is produced by the opening words 'we are proud to announce'?
questions.context: Text: 'We are proud to announce that our new centre will serve families from the whole province, not only from the town where it stands.'

options.text: A celebratory and promotional tone
options.feedback: The formula announces good news with visible satisfaction and is standard promotional language.

options.text: A cautious and tentative tone
options.feedback: A cautious text would qualify and hedge rather than celebrate.

options.text: A regretful and apologetic tone
options.feedback: No apology or regret appears anywhere in the sentence.

options.text: A purely technical tone
options.feedback: The formula is a social convention and carries an attitude, not merely technical information.

questions.explanation:
Formulaic openings are reliable tone indicators. Phrases such as 'we are pleased to announce' and 'we are proud to' belong to a register whose purpose is to build a favourable impression.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the word 'Although' do at the start of this sentence?
questions.context: Text: 'Although the trial was approved, several residents objected, and their objections were recorded in the minutes.'

options.text: It concedes a fact that runs against what follows
options.feedback: A concessive connector sets up an expectation that the following clause will contrast with it.

options.text: It introduces a consequence of the approval
options.feedback: A consequence would be introduced by 'so' or 'as a result'.

options.text: It gives a reason for the objections
options.feedback: A reason would be introduced by 'because', and the objections are not presented as a reason for the approval.

options.text: It introduces an example of a general rule
options.feedback: An example would be introduced by 'for example' or 'such as'.

questions.explanation:
Concession in a single text often signals that the writer is managing a point of view, since the reader is being walked through the two sides of a contested matter.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why does the author place the private statement after the official one?
questions.context: Text: 'Officials estimate that the repairs will take four months. Contractors have said privately that the work could take twice as long.'

options.text: To contrast the official figure with information that undermines it
options.feedback: The order sets the official account first and then introduces a competing figure that contradicts it.

options.text: To show that the official estimate is the correct one
options.feedback: A private statement contradicting the official figure does not confirm it.

options.text: To give two sources that agree with each other
options.feedback: The two accounts differ, so they are in tension rather than in agreement.

options.text: To explain why the repairs are needed
options.feedback: The text does not address the necessity of the repairs.

questions.explanation:
The sequence of information in a text is a rhetorical choice. A disagreement introduced after an official figure is framed as a revelation, and a disagreement placed first is framed as a correction.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does this description accomplish?
questions.context: Text: 'The scheme was extended for a further three years. Participation fell by a fifth over the same period. The report describes this as a sign of the scheme's success.'

options.text: It presents a fall in participation as a positive outcome
options.feedback: Calling a decline a sign of success reverses the ordinary meaning of the figure, which is a rhetorical move rather than an error of fact.

options.text: It acknowledges that the scheme is underperforming
options.feedback: The text presents the result positively, so it does not acknowledge difficulty.

options.text: It explains the fall as a result of funding changes
options.feedback: No cause is offered for the fall.

options.text: It compares the scheme with another programme
options.feedback: A comparison with another programme is never mentioned.

questions.explanation:
Reading a report critically means comparing the label a writer attaches to a figure with what the figure would usually mean. A mismatch between the two is often where the argument is being made.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why is the word 'betrayed' effective in this text?
questions.context: Text: 'Visitors are reminded that the exhibits belong to the region and should be treated with respect. Some visitors, however, leave things behind for others to find, and the museum has started to feel betrayed.'

options.text: It attributes human feeling to the museum, making the disappointment the reader feels stronger
options.feedback: Personifying the museum turns a complaint into an emotional appeal, which is why the word lands more heavily than a neutral one would.

options.text: It describes a legal action the museum could take
options.feedback: Betrayal is a figurative use of the word and describes no legal step.

options.text: It explains why visitors damage the exhibits
options.feedback: The word expresses a reaction, not a cause of the damage.

options.text: It introduces a new policy for visitors
options.feedback: No policy is announced after the word appears.

questions.explanation:
Personification is a reliable indicator of persuasive intent, because assigning a feeling to an institution invites the reader to share it. Recognising the device separates persuasion from reporting.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does this sentence tell the reader about the author's position?
questions.context: Text: 'In our opinion, the measures described here represent a reasonable first step, though further work will certainly be required.'

options.text: The author supports the measures cautiously while declining to present them as complete
options.feedback: The phrase 'in our opinion' marks the sentence as a personal judgement and the concessive clause limits it, which is support qualified by caution.

options.text: The author rejects the measures but is unwilling to explain why
options.feedback: A rejection would not describe the measures as a reasonable first step.

options.text: The author claims to be an expert on the subject
options.feedback: No claim of expertise appears in the sentence.

options.text: The author has no opinion on the matter
options.feedback: The author clearly holds an opinion, since one is stated.

questions.explanation:
A cautious position is a position, and hedging language is how a writer keeps it defensible. Distinguishing cautious support from rejection is a necessary step in evaluating a policy text.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why does the text direct the reader's attention to the last column?
questions.context: Text: 'The following table sets out the figures. Please note that the 2023 column contains provisional estimates rather than confirmed values.'

options.text: Because that column is less reliable than the others and could be mistaken for confirmed data
options.feedback: A warning that figures are provisional tells the reader not to treat them with the same confidence as the rest.

options.text: Because that column is the most important one for the argument
options.feedback: Importance is not what the note describes; reliability is the point being flagged.

options.text: Because the figures in the other columns have been removed
options.feedback: The table is presented as complete, so no column has been removed.

options.text: Because the author wants to correct a calculation in that column
options.feedback: No correction to any calculation appears anywhere in the text.

questions.explanation:
A note about data quality belongs to critical reading, not to detail hunting. Small qualifications placed at the end of a document routinely change how its figures should be used.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What can be concluded about the text as a whole?
questions.context: Text: A first paragraph presents one side of a dispute in calm language. The final paragraph, written by a different author, states the opposite position with several loaded expressions.

options.text: It has been assembled from sources with different levels of neutrality
options.feedback: The shift in language between the two paragraphs shows that the document brings together material of different quality.

options.text: It was written by a single author in a consistent tone
options.feedback: A single author would not be expected to shift register so sharply between the opening and the close.

options.text: The last paragraph should be removed as irrelevant
options.feedback: Removing a position would defeat the purpose of presenting a dispute.

options.text: The two paragraphs report the same facts
options.feedback: The two paragraphs take opposite positions, so they cannot report identical facts.

questions.explanation:
Consistency of tone is a test of whether a document has been edited as a single piece. A marked change in register signals material assembled from elsewhere, which affects how much weight the whole document carries.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the main weakness in the tone of this text?
questions.context: Text: 'Every teacher knows that homework matters. As a result, schools should require more of it.'

options.text: It treats a common belief as established fact and presses a conclusion the reader is expected to accept
options.feedback: Presenting a widely held belief as common knowledge lets the writer avoid justifying the recommendation.

options.text: It uses technical vocabulary that only specialists can follow
options.feedback: The sentence is plain in vocabulary and contains no specialist terminology.

options.text: It gives too many examples to be clear
options.feedback: A single example is given, so the problem is not an excess of examples.

options.text: It is written in the past tense throughout
options.feedback: The sentence is in the present tense, and tense is not the issue raised.

questions.explanation:
When a recommendation is justified only by what everyone supposedly thinks, the argument asks to be accepted rather than argued with. Naming that move is the first step towards a counterargument.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does this tell the reader about the organisation of the text?
questions.context: Text: 'This section describes what happened. The next section explains why it mattered, and it says so explicitly at the beginning.'

options.text: The author separates the record of events from their interpretation
options.feedback: Two labelled sections with distinct functions show deliberate organisation rather than uncertainty.

options.text: The author has not decided how to organise the material
options.feedback: The announcement of purpose demonstrates planning, not indecision.

options.text: The author repeats the same content in two sections
options.feedback: Describing and interpreting are different activities, so the content is not repeated.

options.text: The author is uncertain about the facts
options.feedback: Certainty about the facts is not what the labels reveal.

questions.explanation:
When a text announces the function of each section, a reader can decide where to focus. This structural signposting is a feature of well-organised writing and of good exam technique in reverse.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does this text do, and what is missing from it?
questions.context: Text: A charity asks for donations in a letter that opens with a child's photograph and closes with bank details. The body gives two statistics about the need and nothing about how funds are spent.

options.text: It is a fundraising appeal that establishes urgency without accounting for the money
options.feedback: An emotional opening, statistics about need and a request for payment form an appeal, and the absence of information about spending is a genuine gap in it.

options.text: It is an informational report that compares two charities
options.feedback: No comparison with another organisation appears in the text.

options.text: It is a scientific paper that presents original data
options.feedback: No research question, method or data are presented.

options.text: It is a news report that gives an impartial account
options.feedback: An impartial account would not open with an image designed to prompt a donation.

questions.explanation:
Identifying purpose and identifying what a text omits can be done in the same reading. For a donor, the missing element here is exactly the one that matters most.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why does the writer attribute the second sentence to 'some observers'?
questions.context: Text: 'The minister has been in office for three years. Some observers say that is long enough to have delivered on the promises made at the start.'

options.text: To distance the writer from a judgement the writer does not want to own outright
options.feedback: Attribution lets the writer introduce a criticism without asserting it, which is a distancing move.

options.text: To name the people who wrote the article
options.feedback: No names appear in the sentence, so the observers cannot be identified from it.

options.text: To show that the observers are mistaken
options.feedback: Naming observers signals their existence and credibility, not their error.

options.text: To establish that the promises were kept
options.feedback: The judgement is a question about delivery rather than a statement that promises were kept.

questions.explanation:
Attribution and hedging are the standard tools for indirect criticism in journalism. A reader who notices them can weigh the statement according to how firmly it is asserted.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the second sentence do?
questions.context: Text: 'Read this report if you want your money's worth. If you prefer not to think about that, the photographs on page four are quite striking.'

options.text: It concedes the reader's right not to engage while implying that doing so avoids an unwelcome conclusion
options.feedback: The conditional framing accepts an alternative while implying that avoiding it is a way of not confronting the findings.

options.text: It invites the reader to skip the report entirely
options.feedback: Skipping the whole report is a stronger suggestion than the one the sentence makes.

options.text: It praises the photographs as the best part of the report
options.feedback: The photographs are described as striking, which is attention rather than praise of quality.

options.text: It warns that the report contains upsetting images
options.feedback: A warning would state that content is upsetting; the sentence asks the reader to avoid thinking instead.

questions.explanation:
Rhetorical questions and conditionals often do more work than the sentence they appear in. Here the second sentence concedes a preference in order to make refusing it look unreasonable.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the opening sentence?
questions.context: Text: 'There is no single explanation for the decline. Three factors appear to contribute, and the researchers discuss each in turn.'

options.text: To warn the reader against looking for one cause and to prepare for a multi-causal discussion
options.feedback: Rejecting a single explanation and then listing several factors is the standard opening of a multi-causal discussion.

options.text: To deny that any cause exists
options.feedback: A denial of all causation would not be followed by three factors being discussed.

options.text: To announce that the research failed
options.feedback: No failure is reported; the study proceeds to discuss three factors.

options.text: To introduce a single explanation that follows
options.feedback: The sentence explicitly says there is no single explanation.

questions.explanation:
An opening sentence often frames everything that follows. This item asks the student to read the frame rather than the content, which is a habit that pays off in every genre.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which observation about this document is most accurate?
questions.context: Text: A public health leaflet states that the vaccine is 'completely safe' in bold type, then lists in small type a range of reported side effects.

options.text: The visual presentation encourages a reading that the detailed text does not support
options.feedback: Typography steers attention, so an absolute claim in bold and qualifications in small type produces a distorted overall impression.

options.text: The leaflet is internally consistent because side effects are listed
options.feedback: Listing side effects while claiming complete safety is a tension, not a consistency.

options.text: The bold type is used to make the side effects easier to read
options.feedback: The bold applies to the claim of safety, not to the list of effects.

options.text: The leaflet shows that the vaccine has no side effects
options.feedback: A list of reported side effects contradicts a claim that none exist.

questions.explanation: Layout is part of the message. The final item asks the student to notice that how a text presents information can matter as much as what it says, which is the most advanced point in this area.
questions.subject: ingles
